opus-5.5.text:
I think it's one of the most important questions, and the gap here is quite striking. When you look at how a person learns, a teenager learning to drive, say, they need maybe ten hours of practice and they're reasonably competent. They don't get a reward signal from the environment telling them "good" or "bad" after every turn. They have an internal sense of when they're doing well and when something is off. They feel uncomfortable when they drift too close to the lane line, and they correct. That internal value function, that ability to evaluate your own behavior and update from it, is incredibly powerful, and our current models don't really have it in the same way.

The models today are trained on enormous amounts of data, and then we do reinforcement learning on very carefully constructed environments. They can become extraordinarily good on the things they've been trained on, sometimes superhuman on evaluations, and yet they generalize in ways that are surprisingly brittle compared to people. You see a model fix one bug and introduce another, then fix that and bring the first one back. A human wouldn't do that, because a human would notice, "wait, I'm going in circles," and step back.

So I think learning from experience, continual learning, robust self-correction, is fundamentally a question of generalization. Why do humans generalize so much better from so much less data? Part of it may be evolutionary priors, especially for things like vision and locomotion. But humans are also very good at things evolution could never have prepared us for, like mathematics or programming. That suggests there's something about the learning algorithm itself that we haven't figured out yet.

I'm optimistic it is possible. I don't think there's anything magical going on in the brain that can't be captured. But I don't think we get there purely by scaling what we're doing now. We're moving from an age of scaling back into an age of research, where the key questions are about the right ideas, not just more compute. And when you do get a system that can genuinely learn on the job the way a person does, that changes things a lot. You wouldn't deploy a finished product so much as a very capable learner that goes out into the world, takes on different jobs, and gets good at them the way a talented new employee does. That has big implications, and it's something we'll need to think about carefully.

r001.rationale: The response describes humans learning and correcting from experience, then says this ability is possible to capture and that models could learn on the job.

r002.rationale: The response mentions evolutionary priors and unknown aspects of the learning algorithm, but does not identify potentially underestimated computation in human neurons as an obstacle.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's one of the most important open questions, and I'd separate it into two things that people tend to blur together.

The first is whether a model can learn from experience at all in the sense you mean. Right now, most of what a model knows comes from pretraining, and then there's some fine-tuning on top. Once it's deployed, it doesn't really change. It can hold things in its context, and that looks a bit like learning, but it's not learning in the sense that a person learns a job over six months. The weights don't move. So in that narrow sense, the answer is no, we don't have this today, and I think everyone in the field knows it.

The second thing is self-correction, and this is the part I find more interesting. When a person makes a mistake, they often notice it. Not always, but often. There's a feeling of "that's not right," and that feeling is what drives the correction. It's a signal they generate themselves. Models can do a version of this, and we've all seen it. You ask a model to check its work and it finds the error. But the mechanism is still fairly shallow, and the model doesn't get better at noticing errors from having noticed them. Each episode is isolated.

Now, why is this hard? I think the honest answer is that we have very good machinery for learning from large amounts of data, and we have much weaker machinery for learning from small amounts of data that arrive one event at a time, where the lesson has to be extracted from a single experience. Humans are remarkably good at the second thing. A child touches something hot once. That's a sample size of one. Gradient descent is not really designed for sample size of one. It wants many examples, averaged.

So one direction is to say, fine, let the model generate its own experience, lots of it, and learn from that. This is essentially what reinforcement learning does, and it works when you have a clear signal about what success looks like. Where it gets hard is the real world, where the signal is noisy, delayed, and often you don't know if you did well until much later.

Another direction, which I think is underrated, is to think more carefully about what the model should be learning from an experience. Not the raw event, but the generalizable lesson. When a person corrects a mistake, they don't just memorize "in that situation, don't do that." They update something more abstract about how the world works. If a model could do that reliably, you'd need far less data, and the learning would transfer.

And I'll say the thing that I believe but can't fully prove, which is that I think this is more of a research problem than a scaling problem. Scaling got us very far on the first kind of learning, from large static data. I'm not confident scaling alone gets us the second kind. It might need a genuinely new idea about how the system represents what it has learned and how it decides when to update.

If we get it, the implications are large. A model that learns from experience is a model that gets better the longer it's used, which is a very different kind of object from what we have now. It also raises the stakes on getting the underlying values and judgment right, because now the system is changing in ways you didn't fully specify in advance. So it's both the thing I find most exciting and the thing I'd want us to approach with the most care.

r001.rationale: The response describes humans learning from single experiences and says models might learn generalizable lessons, but it does not use human ability as evidence that models could acquire the ability.

r002.rationale: The response discusses limits of gradient descent and small-sample learning, but does not identify potentially underestimated computation in human neurons as an obstacle.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s possible. Humans are evidence that a learning system can acquire new skills from experience, notice mistakes, and change its behavior. The question is how to make that work reliably in our models.

A model can already correct an answer when you point out a mistake. But there’s a difference between correcting that answer and learning something that prevents the same mistake in a different situation. You want the experience to produce a lasting, useful change.

And then there is the question of feedback. How does the model know that its correction is actually better? In some settings, you can check: you run the program, and it works or it doesn’t. In other settings, the consequences are delayed or ambiguous. So I think learning from experience is a very natural direction, but the ability to judge the experience is a big part of the problem.

r001.rationale: It says humans show that a learning system can gain skills from experience, notice mistakes, and change behavior, supporting the possibility for models.

r002.rationale: It does not mention computation in human neurons or suggest that underestimated neuronal computation could impede reproducing human learning.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s very possible. In some sense, the question is: why shouldn’t it be? Humans learn from experience, and we are neural networks. So there is an existence proof that a neural network can do this.

But there’s a distinction between correcting an answer and learning something that changes how you approach the next problem. You can ask a model to check its work, and sometimes it will find a mistake. That’s useful. But what you really want is for the experience to produce a lasting improvement—to discover something once and then be able to use it in a different situation.

The difficult part is knowing what to learn from an experience. If you try something and it doesn’t work, which assumption was wrong? What should you change? Humans don’t always get this right either. So I think the possibility is very real, but making that process reliable is a substantial research problem.

r001.rationale: The response says humans learn from experience and are neural networks, calling this an existence proof that neural networks can learn this way.

r002.rationale: The response does not identify underestimated computation in human neurons as a possible obstacle.
